title: TB1-04560
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of China who seeks refugee protection pursuant to subsections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The complete story alleging the basis of the claimant's fears are captured in the Personal Information Form (PIF).2 The claimant alleges that she was involved in an underground Christian movement and that in XXXX 2011 the Public Security Bureau, P.S.B were looking for the claimant as she participated in an underground Christian movement. The claimant's friend's husband reported the claimant to the police. The claimant went into hiding in XXXX City in the province of Guangdong which is over two hours from where she was residing. The claimant made arrangements to depart China on XXXX XXXX, 2011 with her properly issued passport with the assistance of smuggler to the United States.

The claimant also fears returning to China as she violated China's one child policy. The claimant became pregnant and gave birth to a daughter in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. The claimant's first child was born in China on XXXX XXXX, 2008. The claimant arrived in Canada at Vancouver illegally from the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2011 and advanced a refugee claim in Toronto on March 16, 2011.

The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. The panel also finds that should the claimant return to China she would not be subjected personally to a risk to her life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. Further, on substantial grounds there is no danger of torture. In determining this claim, the panel followed the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines. on Women Refugee Claimants Fearing Gender Related Persecution.3 IDENTITY

On a balance of probabilities, the panel is willing to accept that the claimant is a citizen of China based on a copy of the claimant's passport as seen in the post hearing disclosure received at the Board on May 30, 2013.

The determinative issue in this claim is the credibility of the evidence as presented. On the issue of credibility, the panel is guided by the Federal Court of Appeal case in Sellan4 which stated the following: Where the Board makes a general finding that the claimant lacks credibility, that determination is sufficient to dispose of the claim unless there is independent and credible documentary evidence in the record capable of supporting a positive disposition of the claim. The claimant bears the onus of demonstrating there was such evidence.

Furthermore, the Federal Court notes the following: The Board is in a much better position than a reviewing court to gage the credibility and plausibility of a refugee claimant's story. A credibility finding is not a finding of mixed fact and law. It is a finding of fact, pure and simple. Findings of fact made by the Board may only be interfered with by a reviewing court if the finding was made in a perverse or capricious manner or without regard for the material before it (see the Federal Courts Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. F-7, paragraph 18.1(4)(d)). Indeed, it was Parliament's express intention that administrative fact finding would command this high degree of deference (see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] S.C.J. No. 12 (QL) at paragraph 46). Thus, credibility findings of the Board are to be reviewed against the statutory standard of review provided for in paragraph 18.1(4)(d) of the Federal Courts Act (see Diabo v. Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2004 FC 1772, [2004] F.C.J. No. 2168 (QL) at paragraph 3).

On April 2, 2012, a representative from the Minister of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness submitted a letter indicating an intent to intervene in this claim on grounds of credibility. The Minister's notice, which includes a biometric report is referenced in Exhibit M-1. The Minister made reference to areas of omissions such as countries of travel, passport(s) used to travel to the U.S.A with a Visa, not answering truthfully with respect to applying for and obtaining a U.S.A Visa and concerns with statements made in certain paragraphs of the PIF narrative. The Minister provided a Biometric report which is agreed upon information sharing between Canada and the United States as well as other countries to confirm identity via fingerprint exchanges.

On April 17, 2013, the merits of the claim was heard and at the end of the hearing, the panel asked the claimant to provide her passport which was used to travel to the United States, proof of employment, as well as pays tubs from XXXX 2010-XXXX 2011. The panel gave counsel and the claimant until May 31, 2013 to provide the documentation sought and for counsel to provide written submissions on the issues. Counsel provided the said documentation within the date specified. PROOF OF RESIDENCE AND CHURCH MOVEMENT IN CHINA XXXX 2010-XXXX 2011

In reviewing this case in detail, to determine whether there is a well founded fear of persecution or that the claimant's life would be at risk should she be required to return to China, the panel has grave concerns with the evidence as submitted as well as her residence in China at the time she is alleged to be involved in the underground church movement from XXXX 2010-XXXX 2011.

The claimant states that she was involved in the underground Christian church movement in China from XXXX 2010 until XXXX XXXX, 2011. In examining the evidence and in particular the fact that the claimant withheld the fact that she had traveled to the United States in XXXX 2010 and XXXX 2011; the panel wanted proof of her residence in China during the period in which she alleges she was involved in the underground Christian movement. The claimant provided personal documents as seen in the disclosure, as well as an employment letter dated April 22, 2013.

In reviewing the documentation provided, the panel notes that the letter of employment is not dated while the claimant was employed as a XXXX XXXX or XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. The claimant also did not provide any pay stubs during the period of alleged employment even though she was questioned on this issue.

While the claimant did provide a letter of employment, the letter is recently produced and does not satisfactorily confirm that the claimant was so in China as alleged and particularly from XXXX 2010 until XXXX 2011 when the claimant was allegedly involved in the underground Christian movement.

The claimant also does not indicate how she was able to make contact with her former employer, while outside China with a view of showing proof of employment. If the claimant was able to provide proof of her departure from Vancouver airport to Toronto, insufficient credible and trustworthy reasons were given why the claimant could not have provided pay stubs or proof of direct deposit salary payments with a view to off-set the panel's concerns in this regard. The panel assigns little probative value to the letter of employment submitted and makes a negative credibility finding as a result.

Also, the claimant's passport shows she was issued a multiple entry U.S Visa on XXXX XXXX, 2010 by the U.S.A Embassy in Guangzhou, China which was valid until XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. However, the U.S. Visa, in and of itself does not satisfactorily show that the claimant was in fact a resident of China during the period in question.

The panel also notes that the claimant did not provide truthful details pertaining to her departure from China, with her genuine Chinese passport, as well as two separate "fun" trips, according to the claimant, to the United States on XXXX XXXX, 2010 and XXXX XXXX, 2011 based on the notation in the claimant's passport as well as her oral evidence and PIF amendments.

The claimant was asked why she did not disclose in her first PIF that she had departed China for the United States with her genuine passport on XXXX XXXX, 2011 as opposed to XXXX 13, 2011 via plane from Beijing to Vancouver, as noted in her PIF dated XXXX XXXX, 2011. The claimant indicated that the smuggler stated that if Canadian officials know of her entry into Canada via the United States that she would be deported to the U.S as she has a Visa. The panel can appreciate that persons who engage in improper travel at times do so with the assistance of persons, such as smugglers, who aim to deceive foreign officials.

However, the claimant chose to continue with her deceit and completed the Personal Information Form by signing and dating it, with the assistance of legal counsel, knowing that all details should be truthful as so referenced on page 13 of the Personal Information Form which was again confirmed by the claimant on the day of the hearing.

The fact that the claimant apologized, at the day of the hearing, for being untruthful to her lawyer and the immigration officer when the claim was made, does not off-set the panel's concerns regarding the claimant's evidence. Quite frankly, it is clear to the panel that the claimant was willing to deceive Canadian immigration officials and the Board throughout the process of her refugee claim, with a view of obtaining refugee status and if found out, then offer an apology. The apology offered by the claimant at the hearing for the misrepresentation in this regard, in the panel's view is not genuine and the panel makes a negative credibility finding which negatively impugns the evidence as so submitted.

The evidence from the claimant about her departure from China is that she departed Beijing, China with the assistance of a smuggler for the United States on XXXX 25, 2011. The passport provided shows the claimant was last admitted to the United States on the above referenced date at Los Angeles International Airport. The panel has no idea when the claimant arrived in Canada as the claimant arrived illegally. The panel does know, by way of a copy of the claimant's boarding pass, that she traveled by air from Vancouver to Toronto on XXXX XXXX, 2011.

Regarding the claimant's alleged involvement with the underground Christian movement in China, it is possible the claimant was introduced to an underground Christian movement. The panel though has insufficient credible and trustworthy corroborating evidence that the claimant was in fact in China during the period in question and is wanted by the P.S.B officials due to her involvement in the underground Christian movement. This reflects negatively on the claimant given she has her parents and brother, as well as the father of her children in China who are aware of her alleged problems. The panel makes a negative credibility finding as a consequence.

The panel asked the claimant why she showed interest in the underground Christian movement. The claimant stated that in XXXX 2010, she separated from her boyfriend and was not happy. As a consequence she yelled at her son. The claimant went on to say that she became involved in the movement as she did not have a religion, did not have a purpose in life, was depressed, wanted to believe in Jesus and have eternal hope and that she felt remorseful and wanted to find a way to relieve herself of sin.

While the claimant gave responses that were reasonable for her to consider Christianity, such responses on its own cannot draw a reasonable inference on the claimant's genuineness in Christianity, particularly when the panel has referenced the problems as it relates to the claimant's alleged underground Christian movement in China as well as the claimant providing some information in her PIF which is not true. The burden rests with the claimant to satisfy the panel of a credible fear in a forward looking analysis. The claimant has not met her burden.

If the claimant was involved in an underground Christian movement in China from XXXX 2010 to XXXX 12, 2011 as alleged and is being sought by the P.S.B, the panel does not find it remotely credible that the claimant's parents, brother and boyfriend in China have not suffered persecution due to their relationship to the claimant given she is allegedly being regularly pursued as recently as Chinese New Year 2013. This makes little sense to the panel given how brutal, according to the documents, the Chinese authorities can be. The fact that the claimant states that her parents are frightened as P.S.B are trying to find her does not mean that they have suffered or would suffer persecution due to the claimant's alleged involvement in the underground Christian movement or for any other reason. The panel makes a negative credibility finding as a consequence.

Based on the evidence before the panel, the claimant's profile is not remotely of a person thought would garner such interest from the authorities. If that was the case, it is not likely that the claimant would have been able to successfully depart China with her own genuine passport, factoring in an alleged assistance from a smuggler. The panel makes another negative credibility finding as a consequence.

The panel went on to ask the claimant whether the underground church movement members she was involved with had problems or were being sought after by the P.S.B. The claimant stated she does not know if the 15-16 persons she was involved with in the movement encountered problems from the P.S.B. Given the claimant's parents, brother and boyfriend are in China, it would be reasonable to expect some credible evidence regarding the situation her alleged fellow underground Christian followers are in and whether they are being sought or have suffered acts of persecution. The lack of evidence in this regard negatively affects the evidence as submitted and the panel makes a negative credibility finding as a result and does not believe the evidence as so submitted.

If in fact the claimant was involved in the underground Christian movement as alleged, it would be reasonable to expect that there would be at least one member of the alleged underground church she attended with, that could credibly have corroborated her evidence in this regard. The lack of corroborating evidence in this regard negatively impacts on the claim as so submitted given the claimant has been in Canada over 2 years. The burden of proof rests with the claimant to prove a well founded fear or that she is in need of protection. Again, the claimant has not met her burden.

In a forward looking analysis, the panel asked the claimant some questions regarding her new found faith she alleges to have adopted since XXXX 2010. The claimant indicated that she attended the underground church in China once per week, sang hymns and read passages from the bible. In Canada, the claimant alleges she attends church and engages in bible study weekly at the Living Stone Assembly in Toronto. A copy of the claimant's Baptismal certificate and her Canadian daughter's certificate of dedication is in Exhibit C-5, pages 37-38.

The claimant has endeavored to provide corroborating evidence that she is a Christian now and that if required to return to China her life would be at risk based on the problems in the past as noted and that she could not freely practice her faith in the future. However, the claimant's baptismal certificate and certificate of dedication for her daughter does not on its own show a genuineness of faith which is a concern to the panel. The panel is of this viewpoint given the steps the claimant took to deceive the panel in regards to her travels from China with her genuine Chinese passport and the like before Canadian immigration officials to obtain a positive determination.

The panel is not sufficiently convinced that the claimant is a genuine Christian based on the totality of the evidence. The fact that the claimant attends church in Canada and engages in bible study does not necessarily indicate that the claimant is a genuine Christian. The panel also was not provided with any corroborating evidence from bible study church members as well as from the church reverend as to the claimant's attendance and membership in the church that may be able to address the claimant's genuineness in her alleged new found faith. The panel makes a negative credibility finding.

The panel recognizes that the claimant submitted evidence to corroborate her claim. Corroborating evidence is not always required to establish a credible claim to persecution. However, when credibility is an issue as it is in this claim, credible corroborating evidence regarding the claim would have been helpful. The following Federal Court case in Bhagat,5 states the following: Corroborating evidence is not always necessary to establish the applicant's subjective fear. The Board, however, determined that in the particular circumstances of this case, corroborating evidence of persecution was expected. An absence of corroborating evidence, then, permitted it to make a negative inference against credibility of the applicant. The respondent relies on Sheik v. Canada (M.E.I.) (C.A.), [1990] 3 F.C. 238, at page 244, for its argument that the Board did not err in law when making that conclusion: The concept of "credible evidence" is not, of course, the same as that of the credibility of the applicant, but it is obvious that where the only evidence before a tribunal linking the applicant to his claim is that of the applicant himself (in addition, perhaps, to "country reports" from which nothing about the applicant's claim can be directly deduced), a tribunal's perception that he is not a credible witness effectively amounts to a finding that there is no credible evidence on which the second-level tribunal could allow his claim. In Adu v. Canada (M.E.I.), [1995] F.C.J. No. 114 (QL), the Federal Court of Appeal found that it is reasonable to expect documentary evidence of the existence of a law and stated: The "presumption" that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention.

In reviewing the submissions from Counsel in its entirety and in particular the issue of the claimant withholding her U.S immigration history and whether such omissions are determinative; the claimant's failure to disclose her U.S immigration history is not the only issue that the panel has concerns with. However, it is an important issue and the panel finds it reasonable to draw a negative inference given the claimant's actions by not only misleading the Board and Canadian immigration officials but also counsel. Such actions by the claimant were calculated, in the panel's view.

The claimant also stated that she has a son born in China as a result of her relationship with her boyfriend in China. The claimant became pregnant before leaving China and gave birth to a girl in Canada on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2011. The panel learned that the claimant's son in China is not included on the household document known as Houku and that the P.S.B does not know the claimant has a son. The claimant's parents are allegedly caring for her son who attends kindergarten and are angered with the claimant due to having a child with a man who is married. Based on the documentary evidence, the Houku is used in China and required for most things in daily life as well as obtaining services such as education, medical and the like.

If the claimant's alleged son is not on the family Houku and that the P.S.B is not aware of the claimant having a child in China, there is little credible evidence that the son is even able to attend a private school in the absence of the claimant. Also, if the claimant's son is not on the Houku, there is little credible evidence available that would suggest that the authorities would seek to punish the claimant, in the future, for an alleged violation of the one child policy even if she returns with her Canadian daughter as there would not be proof of her having a child based on the Houku.

Even if the P.S.B authorities were to learn that the claimant has in fact violated the one child policy, which the panel does not believe is the case, the claimant would likely be subject to a fine. Although the documentary evidence indicates that fines can be several times more than the average in some cases, the claimant appears to have access to significant amounts of money given that she managed to pay 150,000 RMB or $20,000 USD for the services of a smuggler and then paid 20,000 RMB on XXXX XXXX, 2013 to the smuggler to have her passport returned to her. The panel has not been sufficiently convinced that any such fines, if ever applied to the claimant for violation of the one child policy, whether or not she wants to have more children, would be cruel and unusual treatment or persecutory.

Item 5.16 of the index states the following: Cited in a 2004 report by the Resource Information Center (RIC) of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), a University of California (Irvine) anthropologist who has researched the subject of family planning in China stated that "'in general, people who return to China from abroad are actively welcomed back to the 'motherland,' and children born outside China largely forgiven" (US 21 Jan. 2004). According to an expert on China who lives in Germany, cited in the report on China of the 10th Country of Origin Information Seminar in Budapest, parents responsible for pregnancies or births without permission in China could face ... difficulties .... But Chinese couples living abroad are not bound to the One-Child-Policy. Chinese citizens studying or working in foreign countries can return with more than one child without any serious problem. In a 23 October 2008 presentation at the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) of Canada's Calgary office, an associate professor and Mactaggart Research Chair of the China Institute at the University of Alberta likewise noted that Chinese nationals who have children while abroad may not be subject to the one-child policy. News sources report that there is an emerging class of rich Chinese citizens who simply pay a fine or travel overseas to have additional children.

Quite frankly, the panel has not been sufficiently convinced that the claimant was involved in an underground Christian movement in China as alleged. Also, the panel is not sufficiently satisfied that the claimant is a genuine Christian today and that if she has in fact violated the one child policy that such alleged actions against her by the authorities would be tantamount to persecution or that the claimant's life would be at risk. The panel disbelieves the evidence as submitted based on the totality of the evidence.

Simply, after reviewing all the evidence, inclusive of counsel's written submissions as it pertains to a well-founded fear of persecution or that the claimant is in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the IRPA, there has not been a successful argument made to suggest a positive determination in this regard.

In Li,7 the Federal Court stated "pursuant to subsection 97(1) there must be persuasive evidence that is on a balance of probabilities establishing the facts on which a claimant relies, to say that he or she faces a substantial danger of being tortured on his or her return. Second, the danger or risk must be such that it is more likely than not that he or she would be tortured or subjected to other cruel or other degrading treatments." This is not the case in this claim.

In Bouaouni,8 the Federal Court stated "a claim under section 97 must be evaluated with respect to all the relevant considerations and with a view to the country's human rights record." In evaluating this claim under section 97 and considering the human rights record of China as it relates to the problems as alleged by the claimant, the panel has not been persuaded that the claimant would face a substantial danger of being tortured, or that the risk and/or danger is such that it would be more likely than not that the claimant would be tortured or subjected to cruel or other degrading treatments, based on what has already been mentioned earlier in these reasons.

Having considered all the evidence, inclusive of the documentary evidence and the submissions from the claimant's counsel, the panel finds that the claimant is not a Convention refugee as the claimant has not established that there is a reasonable chance or serious possibility that she would be persecuted for a Convention ground or there would be a risk to her life or that she would be subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment should she be required to return to China in a forward looking analysis. On substantial grounds, there is no danger of torture should the claimant return to China. The panel rejects this claim pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. (signed) "K. Dickenson" K.
